notes.1a: Most candidates could score two marks on this question. Some misunderstood billions however, and it is now generally accepted that a billion is a thousand million or 1 followed by 9 zeroes. It is much easier to avoid using all of these zeroes however and to simply calculate that 80% of $6 bn is $4.8 bn (b) Straightforward answers giving two reasons for increased demand, such as lower price and better quality for rice, were surprisingly rare. Many candidates tended to complicate their answers by reference to the supply factors outlined in the extract and thus missed the obvious economic demand theory required by the question.
notes.1ci: There was widespread misunderstanding of the term “investment” evident in many answers to this question. Investment is basically spending on capital goods and is not the same as saving, nor is it spending on consumption. The key to a good answer was an understanding that economic growth increases output and incomes and that this will encourage firms to increase their capital spending. It was however common to see “more money” given as a reason but this is far too vague to be credited.
notes.1cii: It was encouraging to see good use made of the information contained in the table to support answers to this question. The candidates who did best here were those who selected appropriate data to produce effective concise answers. There was a tendency for weaker candidates however to offer explanations where none were required.
notes.1d: Most candidates could identify an increase in Cambodia’s population from the data given. Many candidates however found it difficult to separate the two conflicting trends, and to explain that the influence of net migration (negative) had a much smaller effect than the natural increase (positive).
notes.1e: It was usually fairly straightforward for candidates to identify reasons why building more roads and ports would increase rice exports. The main reasons given were easier access and reduced transport costs. However it was very common to see opportunity costs to the government, such as education and health spending, given as a reason why it might not, but this is unlikely to be the case here: exports by rice farmers are not directly linked to public spending of this kind.
notes.1f: There was a considerable amount of misunderstanding of the functions of a stock exchange demonstrated in answers to this question. Goods and services are not traded here, nor are foreign currencies. Good answers identified buying and selling of shares with the aim of raising finance for investment, but answers which mentioned government securities were surprisingly rare.
notes.1g: The main problem with many answers to the first half of this question was an inability to look beyond the obvious to provide answers which were not tautological: for example it is not enough to say that higher wages make the job more attractive or that everyone will want more “money”. Some indication of the reasons why extra wages might be desirable, such as the ability to meet their needs and wants, was required. It was also surprising how few candidates mentioned the competition from other companies for workers. Most candidates could give non-wage benefits with two examples in the second part of the question but very few went beyond this point to discuss the possible effect of unemployment. However a large number of candidates lost sight of the question’s focus and discussed the costs to the firm of raising wages, such as higher prices and lower sales. Section B
notes.2a: Most candidates could give a clear definition of demand as the willingness and ability to buy a product.
notes.2b: Answers to this question were often characterised by vagueness, with candidates failing to specify the nature of the imbalance. To score marks it was necessary to indicate for example that supply exceeded demand and imply a surplus; it was not sufficient to state that supply was high and demand was low. Unfortunately diagrammatic answers were seldom satisfactory because candidates tended to focus on shifts in supply and demand rather than the imbalance asked for in the question.
notes.2c: The best answers to this question explained how economic growth gave increases in output which would require more electricity for the production process, and combined this with an examination of the effects of higher income upon consumer demand for items which use electricity. It was rare however to see more investment in capital equipment given as a reason here. Falling unemployment however was quite often given as a feature of economic growth but this is not strictly correct: growth involves an outward movement of the production possibility curve whereas falling unemployment implies utilisation of underused resources.
notes.2d: There was widespread confusion apparent in answers to this question because candidates did not have a correct understanding of the nature of social costs and social benefits. Social costs are a combination of both private and external costs, and so equating pollution for example with social costs is incorrect because pollution is an external cost which affects third parties. Good answers were thus few and far between and it was rare to see private costs, such as wages paid to workers at the power station, given as a separate item. As indicated in the general comments above, conclusions need to add something to the discussion but conclusions here were usually summaries of both sides rather than, for example, concluding by indicating that it depended on who owns the power stations – governments or private companies.
notes.3a: On the whole candidates demonstrated a good understanding of the nature of entrepreneurship in terms of risk bearing and combining the other factors of production.
notes.3b: It was encouraging to see a sound understanding of income distribution here, with large numbers of candidates giving clear explanations of progressive taxation. The main weakness in answers was an inability to develop this further to explain how it is governments which can use this revenue to help the poor in society.
notes.3c: Answers to this question were often weak and it was rare to see a clear understanding of monopoly and competition demonstrated. Most candidates who attempted this question could give lack of competition as a reason for higher prices, but very few explained that monopolies can restrict their output and that this will increase prices. It is wrong however to assume that firms in competitive markets will do the opposite and cut their prices – the more competitive the market, the less influence the firm has over prices, and of course in perfectly competitive markets firms are price takers.
notes.3d: For many candidates an inability to read the question carefully cost them significantly, and answers which discussed whether firms benefited from specialisation unfortunately could not be rewarded unless they were linked to the benefits to workers . To succeed when answering this question it was necessary to focus on how specialisation helps workers develop their skills and the ways in which this was likely to benefit them, such as the higher wages they are able to earn. The “other side” of the question tended to produce better answers however, and boredom, along with potential unemployment, were usually given in answers.
notes.4a: There were many clear concise answers given to this question for two marks. The main weakness in answers was a lack of precision, and it was common to see “running” or “managing” a firm given rather than single ownership.
notes.4b: Subsidies are not loans, nor are they tax relief, but a number of candidates made this simple error. Subsidies are payments to producers and the key to a good answer was an understanding that this will reduce production costs. Subsidies can also be used for the purchase of capital equipment but this was only given as an answer by a relatively small number of candidates.
notes.4c: There were some excellent answers given to this question, with a wide variety of advantages of small firms analysed. Perhaps because they were the focus in part a of this question, many candidates assumed that all small firms are sole proprietors and answered accordingly. But small firms take a variety of forms. A considerable number of candidates confused the significance of total costs and average costs. They stated that small firms have low costs as they employ a low number of workers and capital equipment. What they were focusing on was total costs. These candidates often did not consider how small firms’ average costs might compare with those of larger firms. Large firms tend to have lower average costs because of economies of scale. It is true however that small firms are unlikely to suffer from diseconomies of scale.
notes.4d: Tariffs were well understood by candidates on the whole but a significant minority ignored the international aspect and incorrectly focused on domestic taxes instead. The key to a good answer was to explain that tariffs reduce the demand for imports but it was common to see the assumption being made that demand for domestic products would rise without reference to the reduced import demand. Too many answers ignored the problems tariffs cause and there was a common assumption that tariffs were a “good thing”. It is important for candidates to understand that tariffs may damage trade, raise prices and therefore reduce living standards for consumers. This is the reason why bodies such as the World Trade Organisation are constantly looking for ways to reduce or eliminate tariffs and promote free trade.
notes.5a: Many candidates who attempted this question gave an answer which was either too vague or which demonstrated misunderstanding of the nature of the labour force. A fall in unemployment ignores the fact that the unemployed are actually part of the labour force. It was surprisingly rare to see both birth rates and death rates given as an answer however.
notes.5b: The main weakness in many answers to this question was a tendency to ignore weighting when explaining how the index is calculated. On the other hand however, good understanding of the CPI/RPI, base year and basket of goods was usually demonstrated.
notes.5c: Good answers to this question tended to explain how free trade allows access to cheaper raw materials encouraging specialisation and competition. It was noticeable however that a number of candidates also examined the disadvantages of free trade – this was not required however because the directive word in the question is “analyse” rather than “discuss”.
notes.5d: Most candidates who attempted this question were able to produce a discussion of both sides of the situation. Good answers explained the reduced output and incomes and the problems for governments in terms of lost taxation and spending on benefits, whilst contrasting this with the flexibility provided by unemployment and the potential for keeping inflation under control. The main weakness demonstrated in answers was a tendency to equate poor people with unemployment – unemployed people will be poor but poor people will not necessarily be unemployed.
notes.6a: It was pleasing to see an excellent understanding of regressive taxation demonstrated by the majority of candidates who tackled this question, with only a small number failing to explain that it is a higher proportion or percentage of income which is taken from the poor, rather than the amount.
notes.6b: There were some very good answers to this question which focused on the size of firm, the type of firm and the ability to substitute capital for labour. The weakest answers were those which confused profits with revenue and which used the term “money” inaccurately. Increased revenues will not be sufficient to provide funds for investment if costs rise faster because profits will fall, whilst “money earned” is far too vague as an answer.
notes.6c: The most popular approach to this question was to consider a reduction in interest rates and its affect upon borrowing, saving and demand. Full marks however could only be obtained by consideration of at least one other approach and, although some candidates explained how an increased money supply could increase the price level, it was extremely rare to see exchange rates considered in this context.
notes.6d: Although there were good answers which explained how an increased sales tax could provide the government with more revenue for spending on public services, contrasting this with its regressive nature, there was also a considerable amount of confusion demonstrated about inflation. The key to understanding the impact of a sales tax upon inflation is to separate the cost-push and demand- pull influences: the sales tax will increase a firm’s production costs whereas it will also have an impact upon demand-pull inflation by reducing spending power.
notes.7a: There was a clear understanding of a mixed economy demonstrated by nearly all of the candidates who attempted this question.
notes.7b: Candidates produced an extremely wide range of answers to this question, including some extremely odd ones. Straightforward answers required an analysis of reasons for possible changes to forecasts for birth rates and death rates but many candidates concentrated on Nigeria (the focus of the question stem), rather than looking at world population, whilst a surprising number gave immigration as a possible reason, ignoring the difficult question of the source of such immigration.
notes.7c: As was the case with several other questions in this examination, candidates often ignored a key word, in this case “structure”, and concentrated instead on the size of the population. In addition, it was common to see answers which focused on the economic structure of a country (primary, secondary, tertiary) rather than the structure of the population required by the question. Good answers identified the younger populations in developing countries and contrasted them with older populations of developed countries, giving reasons for the different structures.
notes.7d: Large numbers of candidates who attempted this question gave the Chinese policy of one child families as their answer, and many gave no other policies at all. Whilst this policy is relevant in this context, there are many other policies which could have been considered, such as those which would have an appropriate influence upon the birth rates and the death rates. Unfortunately however, a fascination with the Chinese policy often led to long rambling answers which prevented the candidate from exploring other avenues and gaining more marks. In view of current controversies around the world, it was surprising to see so few answers discussing immigration restrictions as a possible policy measure to reduce the growth of a country’s population.
